articles.title: The Best 4K Gaming Monitors: OLED Leads, LCD Fights Back
articles.text:
The question is no longer whether a 4K gaming monitor can deliver sharp visuals and high refresh rates, but which display technology best suits your budget and how you use your PC. Unlike the GPU market, where hardware is now stubbornly expensive, 4K monitors have become far more accessible, with models now available across a much wider range of prices.
The market and our picks have been settled into four categories for choosing a new 4K gaming monitor: premium 32" OLEDs, more compact 27" OLEDs, mini-LED LCDs with genuine HDR performance, and affordable IPS displays built primarily for SDR gaming.
Every monitor listed here has been tested by us, and nearly all of them have full reviews either on TechSpot or over at Monitors Unboxed on YouTube. So our recommendations are based on hands-on testing, current pricing, and the trade-offs that matter in everyday use. Whether you want the best image quality available, high brightness without burn-in concerns, or simply a fast 4K monitor at a reasonable price, these are the models we would buy today.
Best 32-inch 4K Gaming Monitors
Asus ROG Strix OLED XG32UCWMG 32"
Right now, the best 4K gaming monitors on the market are 32-inch 4K OLEDs. Although 27-inch models are also available, I find the larger 32-inch panel size more immersive for 4K gaming, and prices are not much higher than those of the smaller models. These panels offer high resolutions, fast refresh rates, and excellent HDR performance for gaming. With two main panel types to choose from, QD-OLED and WOLED, there are plenty of great options, and it is rare to find one that is outright bad.
Unchanged from our previous buying guide, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UCWMG remains the best overall 32-inch 4K OLED. This is a 32-inch 4K WOLED with a 240Hz refresh rate, and we consider it the best option because of its excellent feature set. It uses a stunning glossy TrueBlack finish that is superior to glossy QD-OLED coatings and does a better job of preserving deep blacks across different viewing environments. QD-OLED has the persistent issue of blacks appearing gray in brighter rooms, which is a complete non-issue on the WOLED-based XG32UCWMG.
WOLED has two other advantages over QD-OLED. The first is better HDR performance, thanks to more consistent brightness output, no panel dimming in bright scenes, and peak brightness that still reaches 1,000 nits. A 4K 240Hz WOLED also supports dual-mode operation, allowing the monitor to run at 1080p and 480Hz. This mode offers excellent clarity for competitive gaming and adds versatility for those who play several types of games.
Asus also throws in several useful features, such as its Neo Proximity Sensor, OLED Anti-Flicker mode, ELMB, and unlocked color controls. QD-OLED does have some advantages, including wider color volume, higher color brightness, and better uniformity. However, we think the overall package offered by the latest glossy WOLED panels is the best on the market.
The XG32UCWMG is slightly cheaper in mid-2026 than it was last year, typically retailing for a little under $1,000. That is toward the higher end of 32-inch 4K pricing, but it is not outrageous compared with QD-OLED models that start at around $800. For those seeking a premium 4K model, spending around 25% more on this WOLED is reasonable, in our opinion.
More Bang for your Buck?
When it comes to value-focused QD-OLEDs, it is hard to go wrong because most offer excellent performance. In 2026, there are two main 32-inch 4K 240Hz panel variants: the original panel that launched in 2024 and an updated version introduced at the start of this year. The newer panel, which we tested in the Asus PG32UCDM Gen 3, has higher full-screen brightness at 300 nits versus 250 nits, slightly improved black levels in bright rooms, and 8% higher brightness in HDR content.
You can distinguish the new panel from the older version by its DisplayHDR True Black rating. The 500 tier indicates the 2026 panel, while the 400 tier indicates the 2024 panel.
Asus PG32UCDM Gen 3
The new panel is better, but not by much, so we do not think it is worth paying a significant premium. When a 2026 model is available for the same price as a 2024 model, by all means choose the newer version. However, monitors using the original panel are currently much cheaper. For example, the MSI 321UPX is available for just $800, while the new 322UR X24 is debuting at $1,100. In that situation, I would save the $300 and buy the older 321UPX.
MSI 321UPX
The 321UPX is the model we recommend in most situations because it routinely ranks as an excellent-value purchase based on our price tracking. There are, of course, several other models we have tested and liked, including the MSI 321URX, the curved Dell Alienware AW3225QF, and the Samsung G81SF for those who prefer a matte finish.
We suggest looking at the options available in your region and choosing the most affordable model with the features you need.
What's coming
When it comes to high-end 32-inch 4K OLEDs, the models we just discussed are available now and are products we would recommend buying today. However, you may also want to wait if you are interested in one of the WOLED options.
For example, our top pick, the Asus XG32UCWMG will soon be succeeded by a newer model, the ROG Strix XG32UQWMS. It has the same basic specs, including a glossy coating, a 4K 240Hz panel with a 1080p 480Hz dual mode, and the same RGWB subpixel layout. However, it is being upgraded to the latest Tandem WOLED technology, bringing higher brightness, DisplayHDR True Black 500 certification, and a rated peak brightness of 1,500 nits. It should become available at a similar price within the next few months.
There is also a new 32-inch RGB Stripe panel from LG that will soon debut in several monitors, including an Asus model called the PG32UCWM. We are not yet sure how that model will perform, but it is worth keeping an eye on because it is expected to launch in the near future.
Also coming as cheaper 165Hz models using both QD-OLED and WOLED panels. These displays do not offer motion clarity as strong as the 240Hz models. Outside of that difference, however, they provide performance that is largely identical to the full-fat 240Hz versions used in higher-end displays.
Normally, we do not think much of the 165Hz models because a $50 price difference compared with 240Hz alternatives is often insignificant. Recently, however, we have seen a model called the Asus ROG Strix XG32UCDS that offers a much more substantial discount. It costs just $600, which is $200 less than most 240Hz models. That is remarkably cheap for a 32-inch QD-OLED and makes it well worth considering when refresh rate is less important to you than OLED color performance.
Best 27-inch 4K Monitors with HDR
Dell Alienware AW2725Q 27"
For those who prefer a smaller 27-inch panel for HDR gaming, our recommendations are unchanged. The only available panel at this size uses QD-OLED technology and is essentially a smaller version of the first-gen 32-inch panels. That means you can expect similar performance to the larger models, but in a more compact format with higher pixel density.
The three standouts are the Dell Alienware AW2725Q, Gigabyte MO27U2, and MSI MAG 272UP X24. All three are typically available for between $650 and $700, use the same panel, and offer excellent value at those prices. It is difficult to recommend any of the more expensive alternatives unless you specifically need the additional features they provide.
The AW2725Q performs similarly to the other options. It is just as bright, looks excellent for HDR gaming, and uses a glossy panel that produces deep blacks. Its main downside is the lack of some features found on premium models, such as USB-C display input. It is usually my go-to choice in this category, especially when available for $700.
The MO27U2 is very similar to the AW2725Q in terms of overall performance and features. I was not as impressed with its highest-brightness HDR mode, which uses a boosted-brightness configuration rather than a more traditional Peak 1,000 mode. Outside of that, it performs similarly to other 27-inch QD-OLEDs. It also has an excellent design, USB-C connectivity, and a KVM switch, giving it a strong set of hardware features.
Gigabyte MO27U2
There is also the MSI MAG 272UP X24, a newer model that we have not tested, though we have confirmed that it uses the same OLED panel as the others. We have not seen any major feature differences compared with the Dell and Gigabyte models, and we expect it to perform similarly to the higher-end 272URX. However, it drops features such as DisplayPort 2.1, helping to keep the price down. With a typical price of $730 and recent sales reducing it to $700, it is definitely worth considering.
Several higher-end models are also worth considering for buyers seeking specific features, including the Asus ROG Swift PG27UCDM and ROG Strix XG27UCDMG. Some of these monitors include features that we do not think justify the higher price, such as DisplayPort 2.1, while others offer more useful additions, including the Neo Proximity Sensor found on both the ROG Swift and ROG Strix models.
Asus ROG Swift PG27UCDM
Finally, while 27-inch 4K QD-OLED displays offer excellent performance and remain easy to recommend, a competing 27-inch 4K WOLED panel is expected to enter the market shortly. We recently saw this panel at Computex and expect it to arrive soon. It uses Tandem WOLED technology, runs at 240Hz, and features an RGB stripe subpixel layout. It may be worth waiting to see how monitors using this panel perform before choosing a 27-inch 4K OLED for gaming.
Best 4K LCD Monitors with HDR
MSI, AOC, Koorui or KTC 27" Mini-LED
For those seeking a 4K HDR-capable LCD, our recommendations in this category remain unchanged as well from last year. We have not seen any new models arrive that would displace our previous picks, the current options still offer excellent value, and, as far as we are aware, all of them remain widely available.
There are three main reasons to choose a 4K HDR LCD gaming monitor. First, you may not want to deal with the potential burn-in concerns associated with OLEDs. For those who use their display for both gaming and productivity, LCDs are the safer choice and may offer better long-term durability.
Second, you may want a 4K HDR monitor without spending at least $700 on an OLED, as LCDs with mini-LED backlights are considerably cheaper. Third, you may simply prefer the extreme brightness that LCDs can provide, with current models pushing full-screen brightness beyond 1,000 nits.
MSI MPG 274URDFW E16M
The models we currently recommend are the MSI MPG 274URDFW E16M, AOC U27G4XM, Koorui S2741LM, and KTC M27P6, all of which appear to use the same panel. These are 27-inch 4K 160Hz IPS LCDs with 1,152-zone mini-LED backlights and support for a 1080p 320Hz dual-mode configuration. Unlike older models we have tested, this newer generation performs well and avoids the frustrating, deal-breaking flaws seen in some previous products.
With full-array local dimming, these 4K LCDs are genuinely capable of displaying HDR images properly, unlike fake HDR products that lack local dimming and are often marketed with misleading "HDR 400" specifications.
A 1,152-zone backlight allows for a substantial increase in contrast over SDR monitors, producing deeper blacks and reasonably precise control over bright and dark elements displayed at the same time. This creates the dazzling HDR effect you are paying for, rather than simply running the screen at a higher brightness level.
KTC M27P6
Speaking of brightness, these monitors are capable of extremely high output, particularly in brighter scenes. The KTC M27P6 reaches more than 1,700 nits in real-scene testing. Combined with good shadow detail and fast dimming response times, this produces strong HDR gaming performance that is a significant step up from cheaper SDR products. Under the right conditions, these LCDs can look remarkably similar to an OLED.
Motion performance is also quite good across these. They use typical fast IPS panels, with tuning that varies depending on the model. The KTC is well balanced across the middle of the refresh-rate range, while the AOC is better optimized toward 160Hz. The 1080p 320Hz dual mode improves clarity for competitive multiplayer gaming, making these versatile displays capable of HDR gaming in single-player titles, 320Hz gaming in multiplayer titles, and productivity work without burn-in concerns.
You can expect to pay between $400 and $500 for one of these monitors, representing roughly a 30% to 40% premium over basic 4K SDR models. As a mid-range 4K option positioned between SDR LCDs and OLEDs, that seems reasonable to us. We also do not have a strong preference among the four models at their current prices, largely because the differences are relatively small. They are typically priced within $50 of one another, with occasional discounts appearing from time to time.
AOC U27G4XM
The main deciding factor is whether you want the mini-LED backlight tuned more toward brightness or contrast. The KTC and Koorui models are the brightest and push peak brightness the hardest, occasionally at the expense of contrast.
The MSI and AOC models are still bright but favor stronger contrast and deeper black levels in HDR scenes. There is no right or wrong presentation, and we would recommend all four depending on pricing and availability in your region.
The other good news for buyers in this segment is that we are not expecting any major new releases throughout the rest of 2026. Based on what we have seen at trade shows and heard from monitor vendors, this generation of mini-LED technology is likely to remain the standard throughout the year.
Best Budget 4K Monitors without HDR
Gigabyte M27UP 27"
If what you want is a reasonably affordable 4K monitor for gaming, with perhaps some productivity work on the side, IPS LCDs offer excellent value. In the budget category, you will not find top-tier HDR hardware with advanced mini-LED backlights, but you will find excellent high-refresh-rate displays for SDR gaming.
The best option in this category is the Gigabyte M27UP, a 27-inch 4K 160Hz IPS LCD monitor. Although this display has an MSRP of $380, it is regularly available for around $330, at which point it becomes an excellent buy. Despite its low price, it delivers performance similar to other 4K IPS LCDs we have tested. It is reasonably fast, offers a well-tuned single overdrive mode, has good calibration, supports a wide color gamut, and delivers acceptable IPS-level contrast. The overall balance of performance makes the M27UP a great monitor for both gaming and productivity.
The other cool thing about this monitor is its 1080p 320Hz dual mode, which improves responsiveness and motion clarity for competitive gaming. Of course, you do not have to use dual mode. You could simply ignore the feature and enjoy the monitor's excellent value as a 4K display, but for those who play a wide variety of games, it is a worthwhile addition.
We do not recommend spending more than $330 on a standard 4K LCD, as the models we have tested generally offer a very similar level of performance in both motion handling and color quality. With the M27UP already well tuned for motion, well calibrated, and, in my opinion, well designed, there is little reason to spend more on something marketed as premium. You will probably just be wasting money, and once you move into higher price tiers, better options become available with more advanced display hardware.
Based on what we have seen over the past six months, the Gigabyte M27UP usually offers the best value in this category. However, there are a few alternatives worth watching, including the Asus ROG Strix XG27UCG, which is a very similar monitor. At the moment, the XG27UCG costs around $50 more than the M27UP, but if it goes on sale, we would simply buy whichever of the Asus or Gigabyte models is cheaper.
Asus ROG Strix XG27UCG
In previous versions of this buying guide, we also recommended several budget 32-inch 4K LCDs for SDR gaming. However, as of mid-2026, all of those monitors have been discontinued. The LG 32GR93U and Gigabyte M32UP are no longer widely available, apart from select retailers carrying old stock. We are also not particularly impressed with many of the remaining options, which for the most part are either underwhelming or too expensive.
With 32-inch OLEDs now falling toward the $600 range while offering 165Hz refresh rates, it becomes difficult to justify spending a similar amount on an LCD with the same refresh rate. Even for buyers who still prefer LCD, there are not many compelling options at that price. For now, unless the market changes later in the year, we cannot recommend a 32-inch 4K SDR LCD gaming monitor.

articles.title: Grafana Assistant Expands to More Than 30 Data Sources
articles.text:
Grafana Labs has expanded the capabilities of Grafana Assistant, enabling its AI-powered observability assistant to query and correlate data across more than 30 different data sources through natural language. The company claims that this update is a step toward "unified observability", allowing operators, developers, and site reliability engineers (SREs) to investigate incidents, generate queries, and troubleshoot complex distributed systems without switching between multiple monitoring tools.
The enhancement builds on Grafana Assistant's broader AI strategy unveiled at GrafanaCON 2026, where the company positioned AI as an operational partner rather than simply a chatbot. By expanding the number of supported data sources, including cloud platforms, databases, observability backends, issue trackers, and infrastructure monitoring systems, Grafana is attempting to eliminate a common challenge facing modern operations teams: fragmented operational data spread across dozens of disconnected platforms.
Modern production environments rarely rely on a single monitoring platform. Instead, organizations typically collect metrics, traces, cloud telemetry, infrastructure events, business data, and operational context all from different tools and sources.
Traditionally, investigating a production incident has required engineers to move between these tools, correlate timestamps manually, reconstruct service dependencies, and piece together a complete understanding of what happened. Grafana Assistant aims to simplify that process by allowing users to ask natural language questions that span multiple systems simultaneously. Instead of manually constructing queries in PromQL, LogQL, SQL, or TraceQL, engineers can simply describe the problem they are investigating and allow the assistant to retrieve and correlate the relevant information.
Unlike general-purpose AI assistants, Grafana Labs claims that Grafana Assistant has been designed specifically for observability workflows. Beyond answering questions, it can generate dashboards, construct complex monitoring queries, explain unfamiliar metrics, navigate Grafana resources, and launch investigations using telemetry from across an organization's infrastructure.
With the latest release, support has expanded to include additional enterprise data sources such as Snowflake, Oracle, Elasticsearch, Dynatrace, Honeycomb, MongoDB, Zabbix, and Jira, allowing investigations to incorporate operational, infrastructure, and business context within a single conversation. Rather than forcing users to learn multiple query languages, the idea is that the assistant translates natural language into the appropriate queries while respecting existing permissions and role-based access controls.
The announcement reflects broader shifts occurring within observability itself. As distributed systems become more complex and AI-powered applications generate increasing volumes of telemetry, simply collecting data is no longer enough. Operations teams increasingly need intelligent systems capable of correlating information across logs, metrics, traces, profiles, infrastructure events, and application behavior.
As a result, like its competitors, Grafana has steadily expanded its AI portfolio throughout 2026, introducing AI Observability for monitoring large language model applications, Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for integrating external AI agents, and making Grafana Assistant available to self-managed Grafana Enterprise and OSS deployments.
Grafana's announcement comes as observability vendors increasingly compete on AI capabilities rather than telemetry collection alone. Datadog has expanded its AI-powered Bits AI assistant to perform automated investigations and root cause analysis, while Dynatrace's Davis AI combines causal reasoning with automation to accelerate incident response. Splunk integrates AI Assistant into security and observability workflows, and New Relic has introduced Intelligent Observability features that automatically correlate telemetry and recommend remediation actions.
While natural-language interfaces can make investigations faster and more accessible, the quality and accuracy of an assistant's responses remain dependent on several factors, including the completeness of the underlying telemetry, appropriate access permissions, and the ability of AI models to reliably generate and execute queries across diverse and heterogeneous data sources.

articles.title: How this startup is helping African founders share data with investors - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Pitchwise is a document-sharing and virtual data room platform that enables African founders, dealmakers, and teams to share pitch decks, data rooms, and other sensitive documents through a single link.
Built by Bantaba, a Stockholm-based company founded by Gambian entrepreneur Lamin Darboe, Pitchwise allows startups to easily share relevant data with investors, and receive real-time alerts when a document is opened.
They also receive slide-level analytics like time spent per slide, completion rate, and return visits; granular access permissions; email whitelisting; and dynamic watermarking.
“It’s positioned as a founder-friendly cost alternative to tools like DocSend with comparable functionality at a fraction of the price. The platform is GDPR and CCPA compliant, with documents encrypted in transit and at rest,” Darboe told Disrupt Africa.
While fundraising is a core use case, Pitchwise is also used to power M&A transactions, sales pitches and due diligence processes. Beyond founders, the platform is used by VC firms, investment platforms, family offices, and boutique advisory firms for use cases like LP reporting and due diligence, and sales enablement, amongst others.
“We built Pitchwise around two gaps we saw in the market – founders’ need to have visibility and security on the fundraising process without having to break the bank,” Darboe said.
“Founders want to know what actually happens to a document after they share it – who opened it, what was read, and when to follow up, instead of sending it into the dark. And they want confidence that their information won’t end up circulating beyond the people they intended to share it with.”
The second risk mentioned, he said, isn’t hypothetical.
“In a case reported recently, college social app Fizz accused its investor of sharing its confidential investor deck and financials with a rival app,” said Darboe.
“That’s exactly the kind of scenario founders want to avoid when they share a data room or confidential documents, knowing who has access and being able to control or revoke it.”
As noted, enterprise platforms like Ideals and DocSend already offer that kind of visibility and control, but they are built and priced for large, well-funded companies running M&A and due diligence at scale, not the African founder trying to close a seed or Series A round.
“Pitchwise is building for the other end of that market – the same quality, security, and visibility enterprise buyers already get, priced for the startups and smaller teams the rest of the market has largely left behind,” Darboe said.
Over 5,000 companies are using the platform, with over 15,000 documents shared and more than 60,000 tracked link views.
“Founders using Pitchwise have closed rounds raising tens of millions of dollars in funding, and the platform has also been used to power M&A transactions in Africa and Europe. Startups have also used Pitchwise’s insights and presentation feature to win pitch competitions, putting the platform’s analytics to work in refining how they present to judges and investors,” said Darboe.
“Pitchwise is positioned to serve founders in all markets, as the pain point being addressed is shared across the global founder community. Expansion plans centre on deepening reach in Africa, North America, and Europe.”
The startup runs a tiered subscription model, with a free plan for basic document sharing with analytics, a starter plan at US$13 a month, and a pro plan at US$24 per month, with annual pricing available.
“We are already servicing hundreds of paying customers across these different paid plans,” said Darboe.

articles.title: How startups are rewriting India's IPO story
articles.text:
How startups are rewriting India's IPO story
The IPO market in the country is not simply bigger than it was a decade ago. It has a different character and discipline now, led by confident, high-growth startups who believe in the India story.
Ask any middle class Indian family what an IPO meant 15 years ago, and the answer would usually be the same. A trip to the nearest bank branch. A paper form with multiple carbon copies and a company name, maybe a PSU or a pharma firm or something your CA had quietly recommended over lunch. You did not invest in these companies because you were excited about them. You invested because they felt safe.
Then something shifted. India's primary market did not just grow. It changed its personality.
The numbers tell the story, but only a part of it. In 2024, India became the world's largest IPO market by volume, hosting more listings than the US and China. In 2025, total IPO fundraising crossed Rs 1.75 lakh crore for the calendar year, according to a report by Blume Ventures. India’s market capitalisation now sits at $4.9 trillion, NSE’s Market Pulse report says. These numbers are impressive. But they don't quite explain why any of it happened.
What actually happened is that startups made investing feel personal for the first time.
Between 2023 and 2025, the number of IPOs of new-age tech companies in India grew from 5 to 18, raising a cumulative Rs 70,000 crore across these three years, according to media reports.
But the more important shift was what these listings meant to ordinary investors. Swiggy, Ola Electric, FirstCry, and others were not just companies arriving on Dalal Street. They were already in people’s lives: in their kitchens, during their commute, and on weekends. For the first time, applying for an IPO felt like owning something you already believed in.
That emotional connection was powerful. It was also, at times, a problem. Familiarity with a brand and understanding of a business are not the same thing. GMP, allotment probability, and listing day gains became the primary vocabulary of IPO participation, with actual business quality somewhere further down the list. By March 2026, roughly 55% of 2025’s startup IPOs were trading below their issue price, as per a Wise Lane market analysis. The excitement had been real. The discipline had lagged.
What followed was exactly the kind of correction a healthy market is supposed to produce. Companies went back to basics. OYO is a good example of how this played out. The company had bled over Rs 1,200 crore in FY23, spent the next two years restructuring aggressively, and showed up at Dalal Street's door only after its core operations turned profitable for the first time in nine months of FY2026. It filed its DRHP shortly after.
SEBI moved in the same direction. Recent reforms expanded the anchor investor pool to 40%, bringing in pension and insurance funds that have no appetite for governance shortcuts. For the SME segment, minimum EBITDA thresholds were introduced, requiring profitability in at least two of the three preceding years. NSE EMERGE has seen 730 companies list since inception and 160 graduate to the mainboard. That graduation rate says more about the real depth of India’s market than any single headline number.
The most telling signal has been who is choosing India. Flipkart redomiciled from Singapore back to India in March 2026, a structurally complex and expensive move that companies make only when they genuinely believe in the depth of the local market. Beyond that one headline, the broader shift is visible everywhere. High-growth startups that could have pursued overseas listings are coming to Dalal Street instead. That was not always the obvious choice. The fact that it now is says something meaningful.
And the pipeline reflects exactly that confidence. OYO, Zepto, Zetwerk, PhonePe, and Cult.fit alone have IPO filings on record worth more than Rs 30,000 crore through their pending IPOs. Flipkart’s much larger offering, still without a DRHP on file, is expected to add substantially more once terms are set. Boat, which shelved its 2022 IPO plans, came back with a revised filing. Behind all of them sit Reliance Jio, which filed its DRHP in June 2026 targeting what would be the largest IPO in Indian history, and NSE itself, now finally preparing to list on its own terms. The queue has never looked like this before.
India's IPO market is not simply bigger than it was a decade ago. It has a different character and discipline now. Whether that holds as the pipeline opens is the only question that matters.
The author is the founder of Pocketful, a stock trading and investment platform.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: "There is a sell-by date on low-code, no-code": What Tines thinks comes next
articles.text:
“There is a sell-by date on low-code, no-code”: What Tines thinks comes next
After eight years of building a no-code automation platform, Tines launched 3B Tuesday, a new platform that uses AI to author enterprise workflows but still uses conventional code to execute them.
The idea here is for Tines 3B to enable employees to describe a workflow, application, or agent in natural language. The service then writes the code and deploys it in an environment where IT and security teams remain in control.
Tines co-founder and CEO Eoin Hinchy tells The New Stack that the company rebuilt its front end, middle layer, and back end for 3B from the ground up, even while its existing business was still growing. The company raised a $125 million Series C funding round at a $1.125 billion valuation last year, and Hinchy says its original platform now executes 1.5 billion automated actions every week.
“Yes, things are going great, but no code, low code, at least to us, was clearly not the future,” Hinchy says about the decision to build a new platform.
“There is a sell-by date on low-code, no-code as a category.” —Eoin Hinchy, CEO, Tines.
For Tines, the problem wasn’t that low code had failed. Large language models were getting good enough at writing code to reduce the need for a visual builder.
“There is a sell-by date on low-code, no-code as a category,” Hinchy says. “It was the right solution for a particular moment in time.”
Low code’s AI problem
Hinchy founded Tines in 2018 in Dublin with Thomas Kinsella after spending much of his career in security and IT. The [original Tines Storyboard] gave security and IT staff a visual builder for automating work across otherwise disconnected tools without having to become software engineers.
As large language models improved, Tines added copilots, AI-centric data-transformation features, and [agentic actions] to that platform. Hinchy says the company nevertheless remained skeptical of using autonomous agents for every step of a production workflow.
In [a set of predictions published in late 2023], Hinchy argued that natural-language chat would replace no-code interfaces. About a year ago, he says, the team began asking whether a visual builder still made sense when models could generate code.
“Building is now commoditized,” he says, and argues that this means that for a company like Tines, the job shifts from helping users assemble workflows to managing the code they produce, including credentials, integrations, and permissions — and handling the runtime.
While Tines started out with a focus on security, Hinchy says about 40% of Tines customers already use its original product outside of security, but those users still need some technical ability to create a workflow. With 3B, the company wants to reach employees in teams such as finance and human resources who can describe the application or automation they need but don’t know how to deploy and operate it.
Tines typically ships a minimal product and iterates with customers, Hinchy says. This time, it built a complete product in stealth without customer feedback and only brought early customers into 3B over the past few months.
AI writes the workflow
The 3B builder starts with a natural-language prompt. The model can ask follow-up questions before generating a workflow and breaking it into individual steps. In the process, users can ask 3B to revise the whole application, if necessary, or just one generated step.
Once generated, each workflow step becomes code that runs in its own ephemeral Docker container. Tines destroys and recreates those isolated environments for every execution, Hinchy says. The code and workflow diagram remain visible for when users want to inspect them (though he also argues that, in most cases, this shouldn’t be necessary).
Once deployed, 3B generates a shareable URL that users can share internally.
For admins, there is a dashboard that shows, for example, which workflows are running, which are failing, which have public internet access, and which depended on a given system or integration. The system will also try to fix any broken workflows automatically and suggest improvements, which admins can then accept in this same view, too.
“’I don’t know anything about Git. I don’t know anything about Vercel. I don’t know anything about pipelines,’” Hinchy says, describing the users Tines is targeting. “We take care of all that for them.”
Customers can bring their own models in 3B, Hinchy says. Developers can also build with an external coding assistant and deploy the result to the platform. Tines’ existing connectors let administrators preconfigure access to services such as Snowflake, AWS, and Workday instead of handing production credentials to every employee who wants to create an internal tool.
AI builds, code runs
“We’re using AI in the creation of these workflows, but that’s it,” Hinchy says. The generated code executes as a deterministic workflow or application rather than asking a model to reason through every step at runtime.
Hinchy says that should make common workflows faster, cheaper, more predictable, and easier to test. The promise here is that customers won’t need to pay the cost and extra latency of inference for steps that conventional code could easily handle. When needed, however, 3B can still call a model at runtime when a task depends on it, Hinchy says.
From shadow AI to “shady AI”
As with similar platforms, Tines argues that by offering an easy platform to build with, employees won’t feel the need to go around IT and build with unapproved — and unmanaged — AI tools.
Hinchy argues that what is happening now is somewhat different from the shadow IT issues that have been a staple of enterprise security discussions for a long time. Today’s employees aren’t simply bringing unauthorized tools into the workplace, he says. 
Many are responding to mandates from executives who want them to use AI, with that pressure pushing them to build internal dashboards with coding assistants without considering security features, or to deploy applications through personal hosting accounts on Vercel or elsewhere.
“It’s more like shady AI than shadow AI,” Hinchy says.
When using 3B, IT teams can decide which systems and data an employee can use before that employee starts building. An access map shows which users and workspaces can connect to a given service and what they can do there. Tines says each workflow also gets isolated execution, credential protection, and full logging.
The same features put 3B in competition with enterprise software vendors and startups building agent platforms. Hinchy points to major enterprise software companies working on similar products and says “half of YC” is building some version of the same idea.
Hinchy points to major enterprise software companies working on similar products and says “half of YC” is building some version of the same idea.
Tines’ advantage, he argues, is the experience it has gained running critical automations and the data generated by years of workflow executions. That history, he believes, helps the company recognize what a healthy workflow looks like, where one is likely to fail, and which controls large enterprises expect.
The old Tines isn’t going away
Existing customers won’t be forced to move their workflows into 3B. Hinchy says Tines has no migration deadline or sunset date for its original Tines Stories platform and will continue investing in it.
Security and IT teams may also prefer the visual builder when they want precise control over a workflow’s implementation. Hinchy expects customers to start new projects in 3B and move existing automations only when they are ready. Over time, though, he believes more customers will let AI own the implementation.
Tines isn’t shutting down the existing visual builder, but Hinchy no longer sees it as the company’s long-term interface. He assumes prompting will replace much of that work.
The visual builder made Tines useful to people who couldn’t code. Now, thanks to coding agents, code is no longer the scarce (and scary) part. Instead, it is now figuring out how to deploy, secure, and govern what AI writes, which is where Tines believes it can take its existing knowledge of how companies operate in the real world and expand its platform to serve them, all while staying true to its workflow automation promises.

articles.title: Egypt's Fincart raises $2.8 million to grow merchant AI platform
articles.text:
Fincart, an Egyptian startup building an AI-powered operating system for e-commerce merchants, has raised a $2.8 million seed round to expand across Africa and the Middle East after pivoting beyond logistics software into merchant finance and business automation.
Launch Africa, a pan-African venture capital fund, and Antler MENAP, the early-stage fund focused on the Middle East, North Africa, and Pakistan regions, co-led the funding round, with participation from Yango Ventures, Five35 Ventures, Bluestream Capital, Hi2 Global, Kalahari Venture Labs, and other unnamed investors.
The raise comes 18 months after Fincart’s undisclosed pre-seed round and coincides with the startup’s pivot from a logistics management platform into an AI-powered operating system for e-commerce merchants. Egypt’s e-commerce market is projected to grow to $20.15 billion by 2031, creating opportunities for startups building software and financial infrastructure for merchants.
Fincart said it will use the funding to scale its commercial and tech teams, invest in product development, and forge new commercial partnerships to strengthen its position in its home market.
“With our strategy focused on strengthening the e-commerce ecosystem, this investment will enable us to deepen our partnerships, enhance our AI-powered platform, expand our infrastructure, and accelerate our growth across Africa and the Middle East,” said Mostafa Masry, Fincart’s co-founder and chief executive officer.
Founded in 2023 by Masry and Nihal Ali, Fincart began by helping online merchants manage last-mile deliveries and reconcile cash-on-delivery payments. Over time, the company has expanded into a merchant operating system that combines logistics management, embedded financing and AI-powered customer engagement. It noted that merchants on the platform can connect to more than 40 shipping providers and access short-term cash advances.
According to Masry, the pivot was driven by merchants’ reliance on a myriad of software to manage shipping, customer support, marketing, and payments. That fragmentation, he noted, left valuable business data siloed across systems, which made it harder for merchants to automate operations. Fincart’s response was to consolidate those functions into a single AI-powered platform.
“Everything we build starts with sitting down with merchants and understanding where they’re losing time, money, or customers,” said Ali. “We built Fincart to replace all of that with a single control panel where merchants can sell more, deliver faster, and manage their customers, without the friction of stitching tools together.”
Fincart operates in a market where regional players such as MaxAB-Wasoko and global commerce platforms like Shopify provide merchant services to e-commerce platforms. The company said it has onboarded more than 450 merchants and enterprise customers and has processed nearly EGP 1 billion (nearly $20 million) in merchandise value through automated shipping and cash reconciliation workflows.
Fincart generates revenue from shipping fees and tiered software subscriptions that range from EGP 1,584 ($31.2) to EGP 7,199 ($141.96) monthly, depending on the features merchants use. Fincart said part of the funding will finance its expansion beyond Egypt from 2027. For Launch Africa, the investment is a bet on the region’s commerce infrastructure rather than a single startup.
“Egypt’s e-commerce market is one of Africa’s most compelling infrastructure opportunities: high volume, CoD-dominant, and deeply underserved at the SME level,” said Lina Kacyem, investment manager at Launch Africa. “The organic, referral-driven growth tells you everything about product-market fit, and we’re excited to support Fincart’s expansion across Egypt and into new African markets as co-lead investors in this round.”

articles.title: Long-Lived Vulnerability in Microsoft Secure Boot - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Long-Lived Vulnerability in Microsoft Secure Boot
Microsoft’s Secure Boot has had a serious vulnerability for most of its existence.
An industry-wide standard Microsoft invented to protect Windows, and later Linux, devices from firmware infections has been trivial to bypass for 13 of its 14 years of existence. The discovery was made by researchers at security firm ESET after identifying 11 firmware images, at least one from 2013, that were known to be defective but remained signed by the software company anyway.
The images are known as shims, which were invented to extend Secure Boot to Linux devices and utility software. Using a technique simple enough to be performed by novice hackers, these old, forgotten shims can be used to completely circumvent the protection, which is embedded into the UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) of the device’s motherboard. The gaffe is the result of the failure by Microsoft, which oversees the signing of shims, to revoke the publicly available images once vulnerabilities were found in them.

articles.title: A evolução pode ser mais complexa do que Darwin imaginava
articles.text:
Durante mais de um século, a teoria de Lamarck foi apresentada como uma ideia ultrapassada. Agora, novas descobertas indicam que alguns mecanismos defendidos pelo naturalista francês podem ajudar a explicar fenômenos que a teoria evolutiva tradicional não descreve completamente.
Em artigo publicado no The Conversation, Pim Edelaar, Professor Visitante da Divisão de Biodiversidade e Evolução na Universidade de Lund, argumenta que o Lamarckismo pode complementar, e não substituir, a seleção natural de Darwin.
Uma antiga ideia que ganhou novos argumentos
Proposta em 1809 pelo biólogo francês Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, a teoria defendia que características adquiridas durante a vida de um organismo poderiam ser transmitidas aos descendentes.
Por muito tempo, essa hipótese perdeu espaço na biologia. Um dos experimentos mais conhecidos nesse debate foi realizado pelo pesquisador alemão August Weismann, que removeu as caudas de ratos adultos por várias gerações para verificar se a alteração seria herdada pelos filhotes.
Como os descendentes continuaram nascendo com cauda, o resultado foi interpretado como uma evidência contra a ideia de que mudanças adquiridas durante a vida seriam transmitidas diretamente às próximas gerações.
O lamarckismo, tal como entendido na época, previa que a prole deveria nascer sem cauda; por isso, durante muitos anos, os livros didáticos de biologia apresentaram a teoria de Lamarck como uma hipótese categoricamente refutada.
Pim Edelaar, Professor Visitante da Divisão de Biodiversidade e Evolução na Universidade de Lund, no artigo.
A seleção natural proposta por Charles Darwin se tornou a principal explicação para a evolução. Segundo essa teoria, indivíduos com características favoráveis têm maiores chances de sobreviver e deixar descendentes, fazendo com que essas características se tornem mais comuns ao longo do tempo.
Pequenos seres vivos desafiam antigas certezas
Para Edelaar, novas pesquisas mostram que alguns organismos conseguem transmitir respostas desenvolvidas a partir da interação com o ambiente.
Um dos exemplos vem do verme microscópico C. elegans. Quando exposto a situações como infecções, falta de alimento ou temperaturas extremas, o animal produz pequenas moléculas de RNA que ajudam a ajustar o funcionamento de seus genes.
Essas moléculas podem ser transferidas aos descendentes, permitindo que eles apresentem respostas mais eficientes diante de determinados desafios logo no início da vida.
Outros estudos encontraram fenômenos semelhantes em diferentes espécies:
- Plantas de arroz podem desenvolver resistência ao frio por alterações químicas associadas aos genes;
- Bactérias e animais apresentam formas de adaptação que podem ser transmitidas;
- Orcas passam habilidades de caça aprendidas entre gerações;
- Corais estudados em laboratório podem desenvolver maior resistência ao calor.
Esses exemplos mostram que algumas características adquiridas podem, sim, influenciar gerações futuras, algo que se aproxima de uma das ideias centrais do Lamarckismo.
“Isso ocorre por meio da herança de moléculas semelhantes ao DNA, chamadas de pequenos RNAs (ácidos ribonucleicos)”, explica o professor.
Darwin e Lamarck podem atuar juntos
A retomada dessas descobertas não significa que Darwin estava errado. A proposta defendida por Edelaar é que os dois mecanismos podem funcionar de forma complementar.
Leia mais:
- Cientistas usam fóssil superconservado para “recriar” o cérebro de uma cobra pré-histórica
- Nova descoberta de fósseis reescreve história da evolução da vida complexa
- Nova descoberta pode reescrever a história do ser humano
A seleção natural continua sendo fundamental para explicar a evolução da maioria dos seres vivos. Já a transmissão de respostas adquiridas pode representar uma camada adicional para entender como algumas espécies lidam com mudanças ambientais.
Esse novo olhar pode ter aplicações práticas. Na agricultura, compreender esses mecanismos pode ajudar no desenvolvimento de plantas mais resistentes. Na conservação ambiental, pesquisadores estudam formas de aumentar a capacidade de adaptação de espécies ameaçadas, como os corais, diante do aumento das temperaturas dos oceanos.
A ideia central é que a evolução pode ser mais complexa do que uma simples disputa entre Darwin e Lamarck. Para a ciência atual, diferentes processos podem atuar juntos para explicar como a vida se transforma ao longo do tempo.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: As US measles cases rise, biotech firms start developing new treatments
articles.text:
Up until recently, measles vaccination has been so effective that there’s been little medical or financial incentive to develop treatments for the disease.
But as measles cases hit a 35-year high and vaccination rates continue to decline in the US, a handful of biotech companies and academic groups have started working on measles treatments for those infected with the virus as well as vulnerable individuals needing short-term protection. It will likely be years, however, before these countermeasures are available, and it’s even more uncertain if those who refuse vaccines would take such treatments.
Fueled by large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah, the US had already surpassed last year’s 2,289 measles cases, and it’s only July. For comparison, there were just 285 cases in all of 2024.
Because measles is so contagious, at least 95 percent of people in a community need to receive both doses of the measles vaccine to protect immunocompromised individuals and infants under 12 months old who are too young to be vaccinated. But measles vaccination rates have dipped well below that in many places across the country.
Young children are the most susceptible to severe complications from measles. The virus can cause pneumonia by damaging the respiratory tract lining directly and by suppressing the immune system, leaving them susceptible to bacterial infections. It can also cause deafness and potentially fatal brain damage. Without a measles-specific treatment, doctors rely on supportive care such as preventing dehydration, managing breathing difficulties, and administering steroids for inflammation. Vitamin A is sometimes given to patients because the virus can deplete levels of it in the body, but the supplement has no effect on the virus itself.
“What we’re seeing now as we get a resurgence of measles in communities is a horrible lack of options when somebody gets exposed,” says Michael Mina, an epidemiologist and chief medical officer of Invivyd, a Connecticut-based biotech company.

articles.title: Vilnius-based Sigvi raises €1.2 million to scale its AI-powered car rental platform across Europe | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Sigvi, a Vilnius-based AI revenue agent for the car rental industry, has raised €1.2 million in pre-seed funding to accelerate product development and international expansion.
The round was led by Helsinki-based venture capital firm Superhero Capital. Vladas Lašas, Chairman of the Lithuanian Business Angel Network (LitBAN) and co-founder of the Carbon War Room, participated alongside other angel investors.
Vytis Šliažas, CEO and co-founder of Sigvi, said, “Europe is travelling more than ever, but the car rental experience hasn’t evolved at the same pace. Travellers expect to book a car as easily as they book accommodation. Meanwhile, thousands of quality vehicles owned by independent operators sit idle because they lack the technology to reach those customers. We’re building the AI layer that connects both sides, unlocking cheaper, greener, and fully digital car rental.”
Founded in 2023 by Sliažas, Ignas Gibas (COO), and Mindaugas Banaitis (CTO), Sigvi is an AI revenue agent for the car rental industry. The company says it aggregates vehicles from independent fleet operators and private owners, and manages all operations end-to-end.
Its AI engine handles dynamic pricing, bookings, and keyless 24/7 vehicle access, as well as automated vehicle inspections, predictive maintenance scheduling, and customer support.
Sigvi notes that it offers a wide selection of professionally managed vehicles, typically priced around 30% below traditional international rental brands, available from pickup locations with no counter and no queue.
The company cooperates with the Kemi network of car service centres, where each vehicle is regularly inspected and maintained, starting from its initial preparation for rental. It claims that it replaces car parts more frequently than recommended by the manufacturer. It changes tyres every season. In warm seasons, the cars are fitted with summer tyres, while in cold seasons they run on winter tyres.
Highlighting its sustainability quotient, the startup says the platform uses existing second-cycle vehicles instead of buying new fleets, offering a more sustainable model by maximising the use of cars already on the road rather than adding new ones.
Sigvi launched operations in Poland in June 2026 and currently manages more than 200 vehicles.
“Sigvi has found a structural inefficiency in a massive market and built an elegant solution around it. We see a clear path for Sigvi to become the digital infrastructure layer for independent car rental across Europe,” said Gytenis Galkis, Partner at Superhero Capital.
The company plans to use this capital to further develop its AI automation platform and increase its managed network to 2,000 vehicles within two years.

articles.title: Sovereign by design: Lessons from Red Hat Summit
articles.text:
Digital sovereignty used to sit somewhere between a compliance checkbox and a future roadmap item. That’s changing fast. At Red Hat Summit, Mohammed Retmi of Core42 in the United Arab Emirates and A.S. "Raj" Rajgopal of NxtGen in India joined me for a roundtable on how 2 very different markets are building sovereign clouds, and why the conversation now shows up in nearly every customer meeting.
Their starting points could not be more different. In the UAE, national regulation defines what partial and full sovereign cloud mean, from data residency and encryption to government pre-screening of cloud operators. In India, there is no sovereignty mandate today; adoption is driven by risk mitigation, customer awareness, and heavy investment in AI. Yet both leaders described the same shift: sovereignty is no longer optional.
You can watch the full roundtable discussion from Red Hat Summit here:
From data residency to full-stack control
Customer conversations have moved well beyond where data is stored. Raj described how discussions in India now extend to operational sovereignty (who runs the platform) and technological sovereignty (freedom from a single vendor stack). Government, healthcare, and financial services are the most active verticals, but AI has made the topic universal.
In India, Rajgopal said sovereignty today is a strategic choice rather than a regulatory requirement. Data privacy rules protect citizen identity, and government-led AI initiatives may shape future policy. For now, organizations are making deliberate decisions about exposure, especially as AI workloads multiply.
In the UAE, Retmi and Core42 distinguish partial sovereign cloud (data in-country, encrypted at rest, in transit, and in use) from full digital sovereignty, which also requires operational control and technology independence. Working with open infrastructure, Retmi noted, gives Core42 more independence than relying on hyperscaler platforms deployed in-country.
Sovereign AI: Models, languages, and borders
AI and sovereignty now travel together. In India, NxtGen supports model developers backed by government GPU funding, deploys Indic language models that can converse in 22 languages, and routes reasoning through open source large language models (LLMs)—all without sending tokens outside the country. The team built a multivendor GPU platform on Red Hat OpenShift spanning NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel, so customers are not locked into a single chip architecture.
Core42 takes a layered approach in the UAE. Its sister company, Inception, trains and hosts fully sovereign Arabic models. A dedicated in-country OpenAI cluster serves customers through a partnership with Microsoft. Open source models run on GPU-as-a-Service infrastructure, with future plans to deploy Red Hat OpenShift AI underway.
The architectural goal is the same in both regions: keep sensitive data and inference inside national borders while still delivering modern AI experiences.
The migration reality
Moving workloads into sovereign environments is a journey, not a project you finish in a quarter. Retmi described common friction points: subjective data classification, resistance to change from security and IT leaders, and the need for phased roadmaps that start with less critical applications. He has also seen customers move data to hyperscaler platforms, only to pull secret or top-secret workloads back into private cloud when classification or risk posture changes.
India is seeing a different kind of urgency. Rajgopal has seen many customers move their proprietary private clouds to NxtGen hosted private cloud or public cloud. This is driven partly by cost but increasingly by the need to run modern workloads on OpenShift and OpenShift AI.
Once customers land on NxtGen infrastructure, their data stays in a private environment where GPU resources and models can power new use cases. His team has delivered more than 150 AI use cases to date, including large-scale public-sector data projects.
"In the short term, we have a massive, almost 54-55% of the VMware private clouds moving to our cloud… I think next year we'll be busy just migrating customers from VMware to our cloud and then adding AI use cases."
A.S. "Raj" Rajgopal, NxtGen
Why the platform choice matters
Both partners stressed that sovereignty is not only about geography. It is about control over the full stack.
Core42 and Red Hat have spent several years building a sovereign private cloud that delivers classical infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) and platform-as-a-service (PaaS) in an environment designed to feel familiar to hyperscaler users, with stronger security and sovereignty assurances. Retmi was direct about the outcome:
"We could not achieve full digital sovereignty except with Red Hat in this private cloud run. We cannot achieve it with the hyperscalers."
Mohammed Retmi, Core42
NxtGen runs its public cloud on Red Hat OpenStack and private cloud on OpenShift. Customers include a Japanese automotive manufacturer and major regional consumer goods provider for fully sovereign private cloud deployments, as well as critical government workloads in finance, health, and elections.
Private-sector demand is rising in the UAE as well. Retmi said non-regulated customers increasingly want in-country backup and secondary copies of data in private cloud environments, —further evidence that sovereignty is becoming a mainstream business requirement, not a niche compliance exercise.
Barriers, futures, and advice for IT leaders
The biggest barrier Retmi sees is speed. AI adoption and geopolitical pressure are pushing cloud providers to deliver sovereign capacity faster than ever. Raj offered a more philosophical view: perfect sovereignty may be impossible for data already collected at a global scale, especially in a country with hundreds of millions of internet users. The practical goal is choice and control over what happens next.
"I really don't know whether we can get to digital sovereignty in that sense, because there's so much data that has already gone away from us. But at least if we can have control over the actions that are being taken, that's a massive challenge." 
A.S. "Raj" Rajgopal, NxtGen
Looking ahead, Core42 is exploring how to export UAE sovereign cloud expertise to other nations through a "digital embassy" concept, pairing government agreements with infrastructure, applications, and operational know-how. NxtGen is betting on people: more managed services above the infrastructure layer and faster enterprise AI adoption so customers are not left behind.
For IT leaders weighing their own path, Mohammed's closing advice may be the one to remember:
"We used to say 'security by design.' We should have this 'sovereignty by design' in all what we are developing. So owning and having the upper hand on our data is having the upper hand on our future."
Mohammed Retmi, Core42
Raj urged leaders not to wait for AI to mature before acting. Security threats evolve daily on traditional workloads; delaying AI adoption risks falling behind globally.
Take the next step
Whether your organization is responding to regulation, managing AI risk, or replatforming your virtualized infrastructure, sovereignty is a design decision, not a retrofit. Assess your posture across data, operations, and technology, and explore how open infrastructure, from metal to AI agent, can help you maintain control without sacrificing innovation.

articles.title: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 feels like the future
articles.text:
Is this the future of foldable phones?
Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 feels like the future
The Z Fold 8 looks unusual at first, but you get used to it fast.
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Samsung clearly thinks so. The company has given its new wide foldable the “Z Fold 8” name, positioning the phone not as a widescreen oddity, but as the new normal, the default design for foldables going forward. Rumor has it that Apple feels the same way, with a similar squat shape widely predicted for the first foldable iPhone, expected to launch in September.
Whether you want to give the credit to Apple, Samsung, or even Huawei (which got here first with the Pura X Max), I think they might be onto something. After a week, the Z Fold 8 feels comfortable, natural, and normal, despite being the shortest and widest phone I can remember using. And thanks to the 4:3 inner display — better suited to both reading and watching video — I’m using this as a foldable more than I ever have with previous models.
It isn’t perfect. Not every app plays nicely with the short outer screen, though issues are pretty rare. And the drop from three cameras on last year’s model to two cameras on this year’s feels like a real downgrade for an $1,899 phone.
We won’t really know the future of foldables until Apple enters the market. But with the Z Fold 8, Samsung has already made a good case that this design should stick around.
The Good
- Unexpectedly comfortable to use when shut
- 4:3 inner display is great for reading and watching
- Impressive battery life
- The lightest Z Fold yet
The Bad
- No telephoto camera
- Still no IP68 rating
- Occasional app errors with the outer screen
Until now, foldables have mostly been one of three shapes: flippy, foldy, and more recently (and rarely) trifoldy. Samsung has played a large part in defining those categories. But the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is among the first of a new wave of wider models.
The 5.5-inch outer display is both shorter and wider than typical phones, almost the exact same dimensions as a standard passport, with a 10:16 aspect ratio. It looks a little odd when closed, but makes sense when you open the phone up to see its 7.6-inch, 4:3 inner screen — not coincidentally the exact aspect ratio used by most iPads. This feels more like a foldable tablet than any previous Z Fold yet, and perhaps because of that I’ve found myself opening it up more than any foldable I’ve ever reviewed.
This stretched shape is more natural for watching TV and movies, giving you a wider screen without too much letterboxing. It’s much better suited to this than the Z Fold 8 Ultra, which barely gives you any extra screen space for video when held vertically and has its selfie camera cutout in the way if you rotate it into landscape. The Z Fold 8 is arguably even better for reading, giving a convincing facsimile of the dimensions of a book when you hold it in portrait.
The shape takes more getting used to when closed, but less than you might think. Even when I tried the phone for an hour or so at Samsung’s press briefing I was surprised by how natural it felt, and a week with the Z Fold 8 has only cemented that feeling. After a while this doesn’t feel like an especially short or wide device, it just feels like a phone.
There are occasional errors that give away that Android wasn’t designed with these dimensions in mind. Once or twice Instagram has failed to fully load, leaving a white bar in the extra space on the right-hand side of the screen; the Withings app once crunched two rows of content together in an effort to fit things in vertically; and even Samsung’s default One UI Quick Settings panel is too long, requiring you to scroll to reach the bottom.
I’m not saying this squat screen is better than a regular slab phone, because it probably isn’t. You have to scroll a little more often because of the lost vertical space, and it can be a stretch to reach the phone’s far side. But there are advantages too: the extra width makes two-handed typing more comfortable (it’s not been much remarked, but this is a pretty similar size and shape to the classic BlackBerry); and because it’s so short, reaching the top of the phone is easier than ever. Anyone lamenting the death of the small phone may, perhaps paradoxically, find they’re a fan of the Z Fold 8.
It helps that all that reduced size keeps the Z Fold 8 light. At 201g, it’s Samsung’s lightest Z Fold yet. It’s slim too. At 9.7mm thick when shut, this is just a little chunkier than last year’s Z Fold 7, or this year’s Ultra, but it’s still far thinner than 2024’s Z Fold 6. Those dimensions put it within reach of a standard smartphone; an iPhone 17 Pro, for instance, is 206g and 8.8mm thick.
Despite its slimness, the Z Fold 8 actually packs a bigger battery than any Z Fold bar the new Ultra, with a capacity of 4,800mAh. That’s thanks to Samsung finally adopting silicon-carbon batteries, a more energy-dense design that just about every Chinese phone manufacturer has long since adopted.
Samsung has been duly cautious in its approach, emphasizing stability and longevity as it’s incorporated more reactive silicon into the battery anode. Silicon-carbon batteries have a tendency to degrade faster than traditional designs, meaning the battery life gets worse more quickly over time, but Samsung says it’s managed to avoid that risk. It’ll take a year or more to learn just how well Samsung struck that balance, but for now I’m heading to bed with 40 percent of the battery left every night, so the extra capacity is doing its job.
Charging is fine, but less impressive. The Z Fold 8 has 45W wired charging and 20W wireless, both of which are good by US standards but sluggish compared to many Android phones available elsewhere. Unlike Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold, the Z Fold 8 lacks the built-in magnets required to support Qi2 wireless charging, though it is compatible with Qi2 cases. In fairness, that helps keep the phone itself thinner and lighter, and Samsung is likely betting that you were going to put a case on it anyway.
That’s a shame, because the phone looks great. It fits right into Samsung’s existing design language, which I’ve long been a fan of for its slick simplicity. I love my lavender model, in a simple, subtle purple, as well as the online-exclusive “pistachio” — though it’s really more of a grayish green than anything resembling the nut.
There’s no IP68 rating, which is a shame, with IP48 protection leaving the Z Fold 8 a little more vulnerable to dust and sand than rival foldables from Google, Oppo, and Honor. Samsung says the phone is sturdier overall thanks to new titanium infused layers under the display, which also make the crease on the inner screen subtler. It’s not quite as difficult to see or feel as on Oppo’s impressive Find N6, but the crease really is a complete non-issue now.
The cameras might be more of a concern. Samsung has downgraded the Z Fold 8 to just two rear lenses, a main camera and an ultrawide — no telephoto at all. And while the new 50-megapixel ultrawide is a significant improvement on what came before, the main camera uses a smaller sensor, lower resolution, and narrower aperture than the previous generation, making it worse in just about every respect.
The photos it takes are fine. This is a similar main camera to the base Galaxy S26, with similar results, and roughly comparable to an iPhone 17. The low-light processing is better than I expected so long as subjects are mostly still, and colors are vivid but attractive. Like many Samsung cameras it finds fast-moving subjects tricky — almost every photo I’ve attempted of either of my cats has been blurry. The setup is improved by the ultrawide, which matches the main lens on quality in almost every shot, meaning there’s rarely a tradeoff for zooming out. But at this price, a telephoto lens wouldn’t go amiss.
Compared to previous generations of Z Fold, Samsung has kept the software updates fairly light. Google’s Gemini Intelligence Task Automation has rolled out to the phone, but isn’t yet available in the UK so I haven’t been able to test it. Then there’s My FanCam, an AI video editing feature which crops in to focus on a specific person. Now Nudge, Samsung’s take on Pixel phones’ Magic Cue, will suggest contextual actions you can carry out in split-screen, like adding an event to your calendar — though since it requires you to use Samsung Keyboard and specific messaging apps, it’s a little limited in practice.
The foldable market is going to change for good in a month or two’s time. Apple’s entry into the space could be the push foldables need to go mainstream, or the final proof that they’ll be forever niche.
Either way, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 makes a good case that this might be the shape their future hopes rest in. It’s compact enough to feel small when folded and wide enough to feel expansive when open. It’s great for watching TV and movies, but just as good for reading, the two things most people might actually want a foldable for, leaving the Ultra for the multitasking productivity obsessives. If I was buying one of Samsung’s new foldables, it would be this one. But while this feels like the future of foldables, it still needs to get substantially cheaper to become the future of phones.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge
Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
To use the Galaxy Z Fold 8, you must agree to:
- Google Terms of Service
- Google Play Terms of Service
- Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS)
- Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.”
- Samsung End User Licence Agreement
- Samsung Privacy Notice
- Samsung Terms and Conditions
There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including:
- Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services
- “Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.”
- Send usage and diagnostic data to Google
- Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant
- Turn on Samsung offline finding
- Samsung news and special offers
- Samsung personalized advertising
- Bixby personal data intelligence
- Samsung customization service
Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements.
Final tally: seven mandatory agreements and more than nine optional agreements.
